howItWorks.intro: Trick-or-treat math comes down to three numbers you actually control: how many kids ring your bell, how many pieces you hand each one, and how much a piece costs. Multiply those together and add a buffer for the kids you didn't plan for, and the total rarely surprises you on October 31st. Take a real block: 65 lit-up porches, a cul-de-sac that pulls in kids from two streets over, and a porch light left on until 9pm — that's roughly 90 trick-or-treaters in a typical suburban pocket. At 3 pieces each, that's 270 pieces before any cushion. Add the standard 20% buffer for siblings tagging along and a late rush after dinner, and you're buying for 324 pieces. At $0.15 per piece for a name-brand mix (close to what a 105-count bag runs at most grocery stores), that's 324 × $0.15 ≈ $48.60 in candy alone, or about $0.54 per trick-or-treater once the decoration budget is folded in.
rules: Total Pieces = Expected Kids x Pieces per Child x (1 + Buffer %)
Candy Cost = Total Pieces x Cost per Piece
Bags Needed = Total Pieces / Pieces per Bag
Cost per Trick-or-Treater = Candy Cost / Expected Kids
howItWorks.outro: A few numbers are worth knowing before checkout. Fun-size pieces run 8-11 grams each, so 300 pieces works out to roughly 6-7 pounds of candy — heavier than most people expect when they're staring at a shelf of bags. If you're torn between formats, run the math both ways: a 50-piece bag of name-brand minis at $7.99 costs about $0.16 per piece, while the same brand's full-size bars in an 18-count box at $12.99 cost about $0.72 per piece — roughly 4.5× more per piece, even though one bar satisfies a kid instead of two or three minis. Store overflow candy in a sealed container rather than the original bag; most fun-size chocolate holds up for 6-9 months, so a surplus from a slow year isn't wasted if it stays cool and dry. If this is a new street for you, undercount slightly and keep a backup bag of cheap candy on hand — running out at 7:30pm costs nothing in dollars but a fair amount in neighborhood goodwill.

faq.question: How much candy do I need for Halloween?
faq.answer: Count driveways, not just houses — a candy headcount is really a foot-traffic estimate. A quiet cul-de-sac with 15-20 houses might see only 25-35 trick-or-treaters all evening, while a street with sidewalks, streetlights, and a reputation for good candy can pull 150 or more. A useful benchmark: a mid-density block of about 40 homes typically sees 60-90 kids between 5:30pm and 8:30pm. At 3 pieces per child, 75 kids × 3 pieces = 225 pieces, and adding a 20% buffer brings that to 270 pieces — call it three 100-count bags. If your street has no sidewalks or sits off the main road, cut the base estimate by roughly a third; if your block is known for full-size candy, add 25-40%, because word travels fast among trick-or-treaters.

faq.question: What is the most cost-effective Halloween candy?
faq.answer: Price per piece, not price per bag, is the number that matters. A 105-piece Hershey's or Mars mix bag at roughly $13-16 works out to $0.13-0.15 per piece. Store-brand bulk bags (candy corn, Smarties, Dum Dums) from a warehouse club often land at $0.05-0.08 per piece, about half the name-brand mix cost. Full-size bars flip the math entirely: an 18-count box of full-size Snickers at $13-14 runs $0.72-0.78 per piece, five to six times the mini cost. The lowest effective cost per trick-or-treater usually comes from blending formats — name-brand minis for most of the night, with a small stash of 10-15 full-size bars set aside for the first wave of kids before 7pm, when parents and older siblings are more likely to notice and remember the house.

faq.question: When is the best time to buy Halloween candy?
faq.answer: Candy pricing follows a predictable curve each October. Shelves are fully stocked at regular price by October 1st, prices typically dip 10-15% during a pre-Halloween promotion around October 15-20, and clearance after November 1st routinely hits 50-75% off, with some stores reaching 90% off by November 3rd-4th if inventory is still high. Buying during the mid-October promotion is the best balance of selection and price for this year's candy. Buying November 1st-2nd gets the best price per piece for next year's stash, since chocolate bought then and stored somewhere cool and dark (not a warm garage) stays good for 8-10 months — well past next Halloween. The risk with buying too early, in September or before, is consumption shrinkage: bags opened out of boredom before October 31st quietly erase whatever discount you got.

faq.question: Should I give out full-size bars?
faq.answer: Full-size bars cost 5-6× more per piece than fun-size minis, so handing every kid a full bar at a house that sees 90 trick-or-treaters pushes the candy bill to roughly $65-70 instead of $13-14 for the mini equivalent. A middle path a lot of generous-but-budget-conscious porches use: stock 25-30 full-size bars for the 5:30-7:00pm window, when younger kids and families come through and are most likely to remember the house, then switch to fun-size minis for the 7:00-9:00pm rush when volume is highest and anonymity is higher. That split typically runs $25-35 total for a 90-kid night and still earns the neighborhood reputation, since the full-size bars go to the kids most likely to talk about it at school the next day.

faq.question: How many bags of candy should I buy?
faq.answer: Work backward from total pieces, not bags, since bag counts vary by brand and retailer. If the math lands on 324 total pieces and the bag you're buying holds 105 pieces, that's 324 ÷ 105 ≈ 3.1 bags — round up to 4, since a partial bag doesn't help and retailers don't sell fractional ones. Buying one bag more than the math suggests is cheap insurance: a spare 100-count bag costs $13-16, while running out of candy at 7:45pm on a busy street usually means either turning the porch light off early or scrambling to a gas station for overpriced singles at 3-4× the per-piece cost you'd have paid in bulk.

faq.question: What's a realistic Halloween candy budget for someone handing out candy for the first time?
faq.answer: First-time hosts tend to overbuy because they have no baseline. A safer starting budget: assume 50 trick-or-treaters (a conservative figure for most residential streets), plan 3 pieces each at $0.15 per piece for a name-brand mix, and skip the buffer the first year since a backup bag of cheap candy can cover any shortfall. That's 50 × 3 × $0.15 = $22.50 in primary candy, plus $8-10 for a backup bag of hard candy or lollipops, for a total of roughly $30-33. Track how many pieces are left on November 1st — if more than 20% remain, cut next year's count by that percentage; if the bowl ran dry before 8pm, add 25-30% instead of the standard 20% buffer.
